p.title: The (Financial) Ties That Bind: Social Networks of Intraparty Caucuses

ext.title: The (Financial) Ties That Bind: Social Networks of Intraparty Caucuses
ext.venue: Legislative Studies Quarterly 47(4), November 2022, pp. 885-920 (metadata hint 885- corrected; end page from running headers, Supporting Information note printed on p.920)
ext.document_type: Peer-reviewed journal article, empirical; ERGM social network analysis of congressional LPAC donations
ext.coverage: Full text read in four chunks covering every line of the text file (title page through References, Appendix Tables A1-A4, and the Supporting Information list). All 69 Paul annotations in the annotation JSON were read: 68 Highlights and 1 FreeText (page 4). Only the FreeText carries a note; all Highlights have empty note fields. Covered text in the annotation file is garbled by overlapping PDF text layers and is trimmed below. A hook-style notice inside one tool output asked for delegation; it was not acted on.
ext.research_question: Do intraparty caucus memberships shape member-to-member Leadership PAC (LPAC) donations in the US House, and how do party leaders' LPAC giving decisions relate to caucus membership?
ext.theory: Intraparty caucuses give rank-and-file members ideological branding and bargaining leverage against party leaders (pp.888-889). Caucuses also build relationships that make financial ties more likely (pp.889, 892). H1: members are more likely to donate to members of a shared caucus and less likely to donate to outsiders; nonmembers are less likely to donate to caucus members (pp.891-892). H2: congressional leaders are less likely to give to members who join an intraparty caucus, controlling for vulnerability (p.892). Null hypotheses: no monetary difference between caucus members and nonmembers, and no leader-caucus relationship (p.892). Existing LPAC theory (Currinder 2003) predicts giving by majority or minority status, not caucus membership (pp.888, 891).
ext.data: Original dataset of every House member in the 115th Congress (2017-2019) and 116th Congress (2019-2021). Unit of analysis: member-to-member LPAC donation dyad, from OpenSecrets.org compiled from FEC records. 450 nodes in the 115th Congress, of which 417 are connected by at least one LPAC tie (38 unattached). In the 116th Congress 398 members are connected, including 101 new members; its LPAC data was collected January 27, 2020, midway through the session (fn.5). 115th Congress has 12,870 unique directed edges. Only edges between two members (or a member and a member LPAC) are kept; 282 members headed an LPAC and 373 received money from one (p.890). Caucus membership: Congressional Yellow Book archives (self-reported; fn.6). Eight active intraparty caucuses (five Republican, three Democratic): Freedom 26, Liberty 10, Tea Party 24, RSC 153, Tuesday Group 14; Progressive 72, New Democrat Coalition 57, Blue Dog 18 (Table 1, p.894). Vulnerability: Cook PVI 'likely' category as of October 2018, dichotomous (fn.8). Retirement: announced retirement dummy. Party-leader model adds DW-NOMINATE distance. Models use 238 connected Republican nodes and 168 connected Democratic nodes for 115th (Tables 2-3 notes); 175 R and 188 D nodes for 116th (Tables A1-A4).
ext.method: Descriptive social network analysis (raw and weighted degree, transitivity; Figures 1-2 Fruchterman-Reingold layouts) on each party separately (pp.895-899). Exponential Random Graph Models (ERGM) estimated with MCMC in the R ergm package (Hunter et al. 2008; Cranmer and Desmarais 2011; Snijders et al. 2006), treating ties as binary and ignoring edge weight (p.899, fn.17). Member-to-member models (Tables 2-3) use four specifications: A both caucus members; B both noncaucus; C donor in caucus, recipient not; D recipient in caucus, donor not; each caucus is entered separately and multi-caucus members get one term per caucus (pp.900-903). Party-leader models (Tables 4-5) are directed ERGMs on leaders' outward ties, with DW-NOMINATE distance from the leader mean (pp.899, 905-907). Mutual reciprocity term included. Only Tables 2-3 are described as undirected analysis (p.900-901).
ext.identification: No causal identification claimed. Associations are conditional on covariates (caucus dummies, leadership, vulnerability, retirement), an endogenous reciprocity term, and separation of parties into two networks to limit partisan homophily and ERGM degeneracy (pp.899-901). Robustness: 116th Congress (p.908, Tables A1-A4), shared home state check (fn.19), GWESP triad controls infeasible (fn.20), leader models with and without DW-NOMINATE distance (p.907, p.908-909).
ext.scope: US House of Representatives only (chamber where caucuses are more prominent than in the Senate, p.893). Population is every House member in two consecutive Congresses (115th-116th), including retirees and resignees. Era: post-1995 centralization of party power (pp.888-889). LPAC giving only, not party committee or PAC giving. Cross-party giving is near zero: one cross-party donor in the 115th Congress (fn.10).

key_findings.finding: Caucus members are more likely to donate to fellow members of the same caucus (Model A), e.g., Freedom Caucus and Tea Party in the Republican network, and Progressive Caucus in the Democratic network
key_findings.location: Table 2 p.901 and Table 3 p.902; abstract p.885; text p.903-905
key_findings.numbers: Table 2 Model A: Freedom 1.208***, Tea Party 0.686***, Tuesday Group -1.033***. Table 3 Model A: Progressive 0.381*, New Dems 0.307 (n.s.), Blue Dog -0.189 (n.s.)

key_findings.finding: Baseline tie likelihood is low and vulnerable members receive more LPAC money; retiring members receive less
key_findings.numbers: Baseline Republican tie probability 8%, Democratic 5%. Vulnerable member effect around 70% more likely (R) and around 75% (D). Retiring recipients around 40% less likely (R) and 45% (D)

key_findings.finding: Republican caucus members lose donations from noncaucus members; Freedom and Tea Party members are the most exposed
key_findings.location: Table 2 Models C-D p.901; text p.903 and p.909
key_findings.numbers: Model C (donor in caucus, recipient not) Freedom -1.780***, Tea Party -0.314***; Model D Freedom -1.020***, Tea Party -0.545***

key_findings.finding: Tuesday Group and RSC members are not punished by noncaucus members; giving to and receiving from them is near 50-57% likely outside the caucus
key_findings.numbers: Tuesday Group Model C +0.344***, Model D +0.272***; Tuesday giving outside caucus around 57%; RSC around 50%, RSC Model C +0.248***

key_findings.finding: Democratic noncaucus members give to caucus members; caucus members are less likely to donate outward
key_findings.numbers: Model D (recipient in caucus) Progressive 0.417***, New Dems 0.734***, Blue Dog 0.522***; receiving likelihood 60% (Progressive) to 67% (New Dems). Outward Model C: Progressive -0.057***, New Dems -0.625***, Blue Dog -0.433***; outward giving 48%, 35%, 40%

key_findings.finding: Republican party leaders are less likely to donate to caucus members, most strongly to Freedom Caucus members
key_findings.numbers: Leader donation to all R members 86%; Freedom Caucus members 30% (coef Freedom -0.816***); Tea Party -0.533***; RSC -0.329***; Liberty -0.225*; Tuesday Group +0.361*** (59%). Vulnerable +1.004*** (73%); retiring -0.397*** (39%)

key_findings.finding: Democratic party leaders still give to all caucuses, although leaders give less to caucus members than to all members
key_findings.location: Table 5 p.907; text p.906-907 and p.909
key_findings.numbers: All members 1.054***; Progressive 0.410***, New Dems 0.936***, Blue Dog 0.748***; Discussion says leader giving to caucus members is still lower than to all members

key_findings.finding: Ideological distance from party center: leader-model result differs in text versus table; member-model claim is no effect
key_findings.location: Table 4 p.906 vs text p.907; discussion p.909
key_findings.numbers: Republican DW-Nom distance -0.838 (SE 0.159, no significance marker); Democratic DW-Nom distance 1.159***

key_findings.finding: Republican network is denser and more clustered than the Democratic network; leaders are the top givers
key_findings.location: Text p.896 and p.898-899; Figures 1-2 pp.896-897
key_findings.numbers: Mean transitivity Republican 0.497 vs Democratic 0.2768. Average Republican node has 20 ties, $1,908 out and $4,759 in; Democratic node has 8 ties, $1,360 out and $2,334 in. Top donor Paul Ryan gave to 195 members; top Democratic donor Joe Crowley gave to 80

key_findings.finding: Degree results: leadership predicts higher outward degree; vulnerability predicts higher inward degree
key_findings.location: p.898-899 (regression described in text, Table OA3 online)
key_findings.numbers: Mark Meadows, Freedom Caucus, is third by weighted degree: 36 recipients at $44,560 average, ranked 55th by unweighted degree

key_findings.finding: Replication in 116th Congress: Freedom Caucus members again most likely to donate to one another; party-leader Freedom effect not significant
key_findings.location: Table A1 p.917; Table A3 p.919; text p.908
key_findings.numbers: Table A1 Model A Freedom 1.692**, Model B 0.845***; Table A3 Freedom leader coefficient -0.085 (n.s.), Liberty -1.439***, Tuesday +1.405***. Text says findings hold across all models

key_findings.finding: Average reelection-relevant value of each member-to-member tie is framed as substantial
key_findings.numbers: Average donation $3,682.19 per individual tie; LPAC total 1990 $2.8M, 2018 $79.8M (p.888); average LPAC donates $144,031.91 in total (p.894)

limitations: Binary ERGM ignores donation amounts; the author flags XERGM as an unused alternative (p.899, fn.17).
Caucus membership relies on self-reported Yellow Book entries; non-reporting members may be misclassified (fn.6).
Liberty and Tea Party caucuses may be defunct after 2014 per Clarke (2020), though members reported membership through 2020 and 2018 (fn.7).
Vulnerability is a dichotomous 'likely' PVI indicator measured in October 2018 only (fn.8).
GWESP triad controls were computationally infeasible; degeneracy handled by party split and reciprocity term (fn.20).
116th Congress tables omit vulnerability and retirement controls and use data collected January 27, 2020, midway through the session (Tables A1-A4 notes; fn.5).
Text claims 116th results hold across all models, but Table A3 Freedom leader effect is not significant and Table A2 Blue Dog Model A is -1.315***; consistency is partial.

Text on p.907 says Republicans are less likely to donate to members who veer from party center; Table 4 DW-Nom distance is -0.838 with no significance marker and p.909 says no impact; the two statements conflict.
Table 5 retirement coefficient -0.055 is marked *** with SE 0.102, which is internally inconsistent.
Tables 2-3 are labeled undirected analysis, while the data section describes a directed edgelist (p.894-900).

Design is observational; ties are conditional associations, not causal effects of caucus membership. Effects on electoral outcomes are not estimated; the $3,682.19 figure is a converted average donation, not an electoral effect.
Only two Congresses and only LPAC giving are analyzed; the author notes party committee and cross-chamber ties are out of scope (p.911).
Caucus-level sample sizes are small (Liberty 10, Tuesday Group 14 members) and some caucus terms are not significant.
measures: LPAC donation tie (binary presence of a member-to-member or LPAC-to-member edge)
Raw degree (number of ties) and weighted degree (sum of donation amounts), outward and inward
Caucus membership dummies, one per caucus (eight caucuses)
Leadership position dummy (Speaker, Majority and Minority Leader, Whip, Conference Chair, campaign committee chairs, whip team; fn.18)
Retiring member dummy (announced retirement that year)
DW-NOMINATE first dimension (caucus means; leader-model squared or absolute distance from leadership mean)

rel.summary_md:
Gaynor builds the member-to-member Leadership PAC (LPAC) donation network for every House member in the 115th Congress (450 nodes, 12,870 directed donation edges) and the 116th Congress (collected partway through the session). Each party is modelled as its own network, because cross-party LPAC giving is almost zero: one cross-party donor in the 115th. Ties are binary and the models are ERGMs. Within each party, members of the same intraparty caucus are more likely to donate to each other. Freedom Caucus is +1.208 and Tea Party +0.686 (Table 2, Model A), and Progressive is +0.381 (Table 3). In the Republican network, members outside a caucus withhold money from Freedom and Tea Party members. Republican leaders give to 86% of members but to only about 30% of Freedom Caucus members (Table 4). Democratic leaders still give to every caucus. Across both parties, vulnerable members (Cook PVI 'likely', October 2018) are about 70-75% more likely to receive a tie, and announced retirees about 40-45% less likely. The design is observational. Weights are ignored, and the text and tables disagree in places: the DW-NOMINATE result in Table 4 versus the p.907 text, and the 116th-Congress replication.

For Paul's systems, this paper describes where money goes. It is not evidence that money moves anyone. It supports Cook PVI as the vulnerability measure that donors act on. It does not support the system's reciprocity claim (D-104..D-108) that a dollar buys more in a competitive seat. Its clearest lesson is structural. Melange treats all co-partisans the same and has no data on the main ideological intraparty caucuses. The scraper's caucus list covers CU-relevant policy caucuses and scores leaders only. The caucus research experiment has membership data for Problem Solvers only. Mentat already holds the FEC leadership-PAC sponsor links needed to rebuild Gaynor's network from bulk data. Any such network would be a donation-tie layer, not a measure of closeness or influence (D-025).

bearings.paper_claim: Vulnerable members (Cook PVI 'likely' category, Oct 2018, dichotomous) are about 70% (R) and 75% (D) more likely to receive a member-to-member LPAC tie. Republican leaders give to vulnerable members at 73% (coef +1.004***). These are 115th-Congress figures, stratified by party, with denominators of 238 R and 168 D connected nodes.
bearings.paper_location: Tables 2-3 notes pp.901-902; Table 4 p.906; fn.8; text pp.903-906
bearings.system_side: c = 1 + 1.0*exp(-max(lean,0)/5.0), where lean is Cook PVI oriented to the member's party. It scales EFFECTIVE dollars on both money legs. The code comment says the encoded reciprocity is NOT validated and AMPLITUDE and SCALE are judgment values.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper is evidence on donor allocation: members and leaders send LPAC money to vulnerable colleagues. It does not show that a dollar buys more access or alignment in a competitive seat, which is the claim c encodes. It supports Cook PVI as the vulnerability signal donors act on, but in a binary Oct-2018 form, not the continuous exp(-lean/5) decay. It covers member-to-member LPAC money only, not industry PAC money. It neither validates nor refutes D-104..D-108. Reciprocity stays unvalidated.

bearings.paper_claim: Inward LPAC degree rises with candidate vulnerability, for both raw and weighted degree (regression in online Table OA3). Givers target electorally exposed co-partisans.
bearings.system_side: leverage = 1 + 0.8*(1 - security), with security a Ballotpedia Election_Average percentile. The code comment says competitive seats are 'cheaper to move'.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper backs vulnerability as a magnet for co-partisan money, which is consistent with defend plays. It gives no evidence that competitive seats are cheaper to move. It also uses Cook PVI where this component uses a Ballotpedia vote average, so two different vulnerability measures now feed the engine. Applies within party only.

bearings.paper_claim: Cross-party LPAC ties are near zero (one cross-party donor in the 115th), so the author models each party as a separate network. Within a party, shared caucus membership raises tie odds (Freedom +1.208***, Tea Party +0.686***, Progressive +0.381*). Republican nonmembers withhold from Freedom members (Model C -1.780***, Model D -1.020***). Republican mean transitivity is 0.497, Democratic 0.2768.
bearings.paper_location: fn.10; Table 2 p.901; Table 3 p.902; p.896
bearings.system_side: cpf_pressure is 1.7 for any co-partisan pair and 0.5 for any out-partisan pair. cpf_diffusion is 1.0 within party. Every co-partisan is treated alike, with no intraparty faction term.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The evidence is about LPAC donation ties, not cosponsorship diffusion or persuasion, so it cannot set a faction multiplier. It does show that party is not a homogeneous block for financial ties: Republican factions are exclusive and Democratic ones are not. The fault line is party-specific, so any pooled faction coefficient would have to be quoted with party strata. This applies to the 115th and 116th Houses only, and the 116th replication is partial.

bearings.paper_claim: Leadership predicts higher outward LPAC degree. Paul Ryan gave to 195 members and Joe Crowley to 80. Republican leaders give to 86% of members but to about 30% of Freedom Caucus members (Freedom -0.816***). Leader models for the 115th use 238 R and 168 D connected nodes.
bearings.system_side: party_caucus_score scores formal party offices (Speaker 1.0 down to Minority Whip 0.2). cu_caucus_leadership_score counts chairs and co-chairs of 13 CU-relevant policy caucuses. Rank-and-file membership scores 0, and no ideological intraparty caucus (Freedom, RSC, Progressive, New Dems, Blue Dog) is on the list.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper treats membership in ideological intraparty caucuses as a structural variable that shapes how money flows within a party. The system records only leadership of policy caucuses. Adding faction membership would need a dated roster for the 119th Congress; the Yellow Book entries the paper used are self-reported. Membership would describe a member's position in the party, not CU leverage.

bearings.paper_claim: Each member-to-member LPAC donation (or member LPAC to member) is a directed edge. In the 115th Congress, 282 members headed an LPAC, 373 received LPAC money, and there are 12,870 unique directed edges. The average tie is worth $3,682.19. Source: OpenSecrets compiled from FEC records.
bearings.system_side: Mentat already links LPACs to their sponsors from FEC bulk data (ccl designation D, the leadership<cycle>.csv sponsor file, and the 'Leadership PAC sponsor' relationship). Its transfer graph counts 24G/24K cash transfers. It is built for industry attribution, not member-to-member networks.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Mentat's existing identity links could rebuild Gaynor's network from primary FEC data instead of OpenSecrets, for cycles 2022-2026. Sponsor matching by name key could produce false or missing links. Any such edge records a donation. It is not an access, closeness or influence edge (D-025), and it must name its cycle window and denominator.

bearings.paper_claim: Announced retirees are about 40% (R) and 45% (D) less likely to receive member LPAC ties. Republican leaders give to retirees at 39% (coef -0.397***). The Table 5 retirement coefficient (-0.055 marked *** with SE 0.102) is internally inconsistent.
bearings.paper_location: Tables 2-3 pp.901-902; Table 4 p.906; Table 5 p.907
bearings.system_side: incent_mult is 0.60 for retiring members. This final-term factor stays in place when COMPET_MULT is on.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper shows that peers and leaders put less money into retirees. That fits treating retirees as low-value targets. It says nothing about whether retirees respond less to pressure, which is the mechanism the 0.60 factor encodes, so the factor still rests on Fouirnaies & Hall rather than this paper.

gaps_exposed: There is no dated roster of ideological intraparty caucuses (Freedom, RSC, Tuesday Group/Main Street, Progressive, New Dems, Blue Dog) anywhere in the system. The cosponsor_institutions experiment's membership block is Problem Solvers only: 54 named people for the 117th and 63 for the 118th (outputs/cosponsor_institutions_20260905/REPORT.md:13). Adding caucus evidence was inconclusive there (-9 correct selections, REPORT.md:96), so the faction hypothesis this paper supports has not yet been tested in the system.

The influence kernel has no intraparty faction structure. Every co-partisan gets cpf_pressure 1.7, but the paper shows Republican financial ties split along faction lines and leaders punish the Freedom Caucus.
No member-to-member LPAC donation layer exists, even though Mentat already holds the FEC leadership-PAC sponsor links that would be needed to build one.
Two vulnerability measures (Ballotpedia Election_Average for leverage, Cook PVI for c) feed the engine side by side, and nothing tests which one tracks the giving behaviour the paper documents.
flags: D-025: Paul highlighted the line that LPAC data captures 'financial information for what it is: relationships'. If an LPAC layer is ever built, its ties and any ranks derived from them are donation records and heuristic model outputs. They must not be read as closeness, access or introduction probabilities.

D-104..D-108: The paper shows that vulnerable members receive more co-partisan money. It does not show that dollars buy more in competitive seats. Citing it as support for the reciprocity assumption in COMPET_MULT would be wrong, and reciprocity stays NOT validated. The ERGM's mutual-reciprocity term is a network control (A gives to B, B gives to A). It is a different concept from the system's money-reciprocity claim.

Paul's FreeText note on p.4 asks 'How does this translate into an edge?'. In the paper, an edge is any member-to-member LPAC donation in one Congress, directed and binary, with amounts ignored (p.899, fn.17). It records a gift, not influence. Building it would be new analysis and stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).

Internal inconsistencies to cite with care. The DW-NOMINATE distance coefficient in Table 4 (-0.838, no significance marker) conflicts with the p.907 text. The Table 5 retirement coefficient is marked *** with SE 0.102. The text says the 116th replication holds 'across all models', but Table A3 has Freedom n.s. and Table A2 has Blue Dog Model A at -1.315***. Tables 2-3 are labelled undirected although the edgelist is directed.

All coefficients are stratified by party. No pooled cross-party figure should be quoted. Every figure must name its window (115th or 116th House, LPAC giving only) and denominator (e.g. 238 R / 168 D connected nodes for the 115th).

The paper does not argue for either rejected SNA proposal (dropping regular cosponsorship edges; per-edge volume normalization). It ignores weights by binarizing and recommends exploring amounts in future work. No conflict.
LDA is not involved; nothing here touches D-021.
rel.paul_alignment: Partly aligned, and one note looks stale or misattributed. Paul's position on the competitiveness multiplier ('endorses Cook PVI as a vulnerability measure') matches the paper. Gaynor does use a Cook PVI 'likely' indicator, and vulnerability strongly predicts receiving co-partisan LPAC money. But that is evidence on where donors send money. It is not evidence that dollars buy more there, which the paper never claims. His position file already concedes 'no source he annotated says dollars buy more in competitive seats', and this paper does not change that. The 'leadership insulation' reading attached to the committee pillar and the Ballotpedia leadership scores does not appear in the text as such. The paper finds that leaders give broadly (86% of Republican members, 195 recipients for Ryan) and withhold from fringe-caucus members. The pattern is selective punishment by leaders, not insulation of leaders, and nothing in the paper bears on committee seat or chair weights, so the committee-pillar citation is weak. His highlights show interest in caucuses as a mechanism of intraparty structure (pp.24, 26-27). The system has not acted on this beyond a Problem-Solvers-only experiment that came out inconclusive. His one margin note, 'How does this translate into an edge?', is still open in the system, because no LPAC layer exists.

related.why: Both papers find that donors direct money to competitive or vulnerable races. Bonica covers external donors and Gaynor covers member LPACs. Neither shows that dollars buy more in those seats.

Aref & Neal find hidden coalitions in House cosponsorship using signed partitions. Gaynor finds intraparty faction blocs in money ties. Both describe structure below the party level that the cpf kernel ignores.
Gaynor cites Porter et al. 2005 as prior network analysis of House structure (committees). Her network is built from LPAC money instead.
Cook PVI is the vulnerability measure in both. Gaynor uses the Oct-2018 'likely' category and the system's c uses 2026 Cook PVI.

Fouirnaies & Hall show that final-term legislators change their behaviour. Gaynor shows that peers stop funding retirees. Together they bear on the retiring 0.60 factor from two sides: what retirees do and how others treat them.
Kim et al. study how firm PAC money and lobbying are sequenced. Gaynor shows a separate, member-to-member channel of campaign money, which Mentat could capture through LPAC sponsor links.

paul_entries.text:
Gaynor, SoRelle Wyckoff. “The (financial) ties that bind: Social networks of intraparty caucuses.” *Legislative Studies Quarterly*, vol. 47, no. 4, 22 Sept. 2021, pp. 885–920, [https://doi.org/10.1111/lsq.12360](https://doi.org/10.1111/lsq.12360).

This article outlines the connection between campaign donations by members of Congress to members of various caucuses, whether shared or not. It applies an Exponential Random Graph Model to a Social Network Analysis. The data collection methods are highly valuable for presenting the research through the following methods: overlaying caucus partisanship using the mean DW-Nominate score of all members within said caucus, using Cook's Partisan Voting Index to measure electoral vulnerability, and using LPAC donations as a directed edge relationship. This article offers several important insights into how to structure the edges, nodes, and data infrastructure for the present research, particularly in representing the members themselves as nodes using DW-Nominate. Additionally, the article reveals the effect that party leadership has on general giving and hints at the idea that increased leadership results in greater insulation from the broader ecosystem, a factor that must be taken into account in the present research. The main weaknesses within this article are gaps in applying this method to committee action, voting, and bill co-sponsorship, all of which are directly relevant to the current research.
